members.summary: Frozen configuration for every Flow Matching variant.

parameters.name: sample_size
parameters.description: Spatial resolution of a sample.

parameters.name: in_channels
parameters.description: Channels per sample.

parameters.name: out_channels
parameters.description:
Kept equal to `in_channels`: the field is a velocity in the same
space as the sample, so it cannot change the dimension.

parameters.name: act_fn
parameters.description: Activation inside the velocity field.

parameters.name: base_channels
parameters.description: Width of the first U-Net stage.

parameters.name: channel_mult
parameters.description:
Per-stage width multipliers; the length sets the depth of the
encoder/decoder ladder.

parameters.name: num_res_blocks
parameters.description: Residual blocks per resolution.

parameters.name: attention_resolutions
parameters.description: Spatial sizes at which self-attention is applied.

parameters.name: num_head_channels
parameters.description:
Channels per attention head.  The head *count* is derived per
block, so a stage twice as wide gets twice as many heads — the
multi-resolution attention the architecture this borrows from
specifies.

parameters.name: dropout
parameters.description: Dropout inside residual blocks.

parameters.name: resnet_groups
parameters.description: GroupNorm groups; clamped down when a stage has fewer channels.

parameters.name: path
parameters.description:
Which conditional probability path the regression target comes
from.  Both are trained by the same objective — that equivalence
is the paper's point — and `"ot"` is the one it recommends.

parameters.name: sigma_min
parameters.description:
Width of the Gaussian left around a data point at `t = 1`.  The
paper requires only that it be "sufficiently small" and publishes
no value, so this is a choice rather than a citation; anything
small and positive behaves the same.  At exactly zero the path
degenerates to a pure straight line between the two samples.

parameters.name: beta_min
parameters.description:
Endpoints of the linear $\beta(t)$ used by the diffusion
path.  Ignored when `path="ot"`.

parameters.name: beta_max
parameters.description:
Endpoints of the linear $\beta(t)$ used by the diffusion
path.  Ignored when `path="ot"`.

parameters.name: solver
parameters.description:
Method handed to `lucid.diffeq.odeint` for sampling and
likelihood — the paper's own choice.

parameters.name: rtol
parameters.description: Solver tolerances; the values the paper evaluates with.

parameters.name: atol
parameters.description: Solver tolerances; the values the paper evaluates with.

parameters.name: trace_method
parameters.description:
How the divergence is obtained when scoring likelihood.  `None`
picks by dimension.  Irrelevant to training.

parameters.name: trace_noise
parameters.description: Probe distribution for the Hutchinson estimate.

parameters.name: exact_trace_max_dim
parameters.description:
Dimension below which `trace_method=None` resolves to
`"exact"`.

examples:
>>> from lucid.models.generative.flow_matching import FlowMatchingConfig
>>> FlowMatchingConfig().path
'ot'
>>> FlowMatchingConfig(sample_size=32, in_channels=3).data_dim
3072
notes:
`in_channels` and `out_channels` must agree: the field lives in
the sample's own space.

members.summary: Flow Matching with the CFM training loss and `.generate()`.
members.extended:
`forward(x)` returns a `DiffusionModelOutput` whose `loss`
is the Conditional Flow Matching objective and whose `sample` is the
field's prediction at the sampled path points.  `generate(n)`
integrates the field from a standard-normal draw to `t = 1`.

>>> import lucid
>>> from lucid.models.generative.flow_matching import (
...     FlowMatchingConfig, FlowMatchingForImageGeneration,

...                          channel_mult=(1, 2), num_res_blocks=1,
...                          attention_resolutions=(), resnet_groups=8)
>>> model = FlowMatchingForImageGeneration(cfg).eval()
>>> model(lucid.randn((2, 3, 8, 8))).loss.shape
()
>>> model.generate(n_samples=2, steps=4).samples.shape

Generative Modeling"*, ICLR, 2023 ([arXiv:2210.02747](https://arxiv.org/abs/2210.02747)).  Reported for

methods.summary: int: Flattened width `D` of one sample.

methods.name: path
methods.summary: str: Which conditional probability path the target comes from.

methods.name: trace_method
methods.summary: str: How the divergence is obtained when scoring likelihood.

methods.name: nfe
methods.summary: int: Field evaluations spent by the most recent solve.
methods.extended:
A training step solves nothing and leaves the count where the last
solve put it.  The number the paper cares about: straighter paths
need fewer.

methods.name: coefficients
methods.summary: `(a_t, sigma_t, a_t', sigma_t')` for the configured path.
methods.extended:
Exposed because it is the only place the two paths differ, and
because checking a schedule's derivative against a difference
quotient is the cheapest way to know a new one is right.

methods.name: path_sample
methods.signature: path_sample(x1: Tensor, x0: Tensor, t: Tensor)
methods.summary: Draw $x_t \sim p_t(\cdot \mid x_1)$, given the noise `x0`.

parameters.name: x1
parameters.description: `(B, C, H, W)` data samples — the conditioning point.

parameters.name: x0
parameters.description: `(B, C, H, W)` standard-normal samples.

returns.description:
`(B, C, H, W)` point on the conditional path.  For the
optimal-transport path this is the straight-line interpolation
of paper eq. (22).

examples:
>>> import lucid
>>> from lucid.models.generative.flow_matching import (
...     FlowMatchingConfig, FlowMatchingModel,
... )
>>> cfg = FlowMatchingConfig(sample_size=8, base_channels=16,
...                          channel_mult=(1, 2), num_res_blocks=1,
...                          attention_resolutions=(), resnet_groups=8)
>>> model = FlowMatchingModel(cfg).eval()
>>> x1, x0 = lucid.randn((2, 3, 8, 8)), lucid.randn((2, 3, 8, 8))
>>> model.path_sample(x1, x0, lucid.tensor([0.25, 0.75])).shape
(2, 3, 8, 8)
>>> bool(lucid.allclose(model.path_sample(x1, x0, lucid.zeros(2)), x0))
True
>>> end = model.path_sample(x1, x0, lucid.ones(2))
>>> bool(lucid.allclose(end, x1 + cfg.sigma_min * x0))  # still sigma_min wide
True

methods.name: conditional_target
methods.signature: conditional_target(x1: Tensor, x0: Tensor, t: Tensor)
methods.summary: The field $u_t(x \mid x_1)$ that generates the path.
methods.extended:
Theorem 3 states it as
$(\sigma_t'/\sigma_t)(x - a_t x_1) + a_t' x_1$.  Since
$x - a_t x_1 = \sigma_t x_0$ for the sample actually drawn,
that reduces to $\sigma_t' x_0 + a_t' x_1$ — the same
quantity with **no division by** $\sigma_t$, which matters
because $\sigma_t \to 0$ at `t = 1` on the diffusion path.
For the optimal-transport path it collapses further, to the
$t$-independent $x_1 - (1 - \sigma_{\min}) x_0$ of
paper eq. (23).

parameters.name: x1
parameters.description: `(B, C, H, W)` data and noise samples.

parameters.name: x0
parameters.description: `(B, C, H, W)` data and noise samples.

examples:
>>> import lucid
>>> from lucid.models.generative.flow_matching import (
...     FlowMatchingConfig, FlowMatchingModel,
... )
>>> cfg = FlowMatchingConfig(sample_size=8, base_channels=16,
...                          channel_mult=(1, 2), num_res_blocks=1,
...                          attention_resolutions=(), resnet_groups=8)
>>> model = FlowMatchingModel(cfg).eval()
>>> x1, x0 = lucid.randn((2, 3, 8, 8)), lucid.randn((2, 3, 8, 8))
>>> t = lucid.tensor([0.3, 0.6])
>>> target = model.conditional_target(x1, x0, t)
>>> target.shape
(2, 3, 8, 8)
>>> step = 1e-2  # the target is the time derivative of the path
>>> ahead = model.path_sample(x1, x0, t + step)
>>> slope = (ahead - model.path_sample(x1, x0, t)) / step
>>> bool(lucid.allclose(slope, target, atol=1e-3))
True
>>> bool(lucid.allclose(target, x1 - (1 - cfg.sigma_min) * x0))  # eq. (23)
True

methods.name: flow_matching_loss
methods.summary: One Conditional Flow Matching step — no ODE is solved.

parameters.name: x1
parameters.description: `(B, C, H, W)` data batch.

returns.description:
`(loss, prediction, target)` — the scalar mean squared
error, the field's output at the sampled points, and what it
was regressed against.

examples:
>>> import lucid
>>> from lucid.models.generative.flow_matching import (
...     FlowMatchingConfig, FlowMatchingModel,
... )
>>> cfg = FlowMatchingConfig(sample_size=8, base_channels=16,
...                          channel_mult=(1, 2), num_res_blocks=1,
...                          attention_resolutions=(), resnet_groups=8)
>>> model = FlowMatchingModel(cfg).eval()
>>> loss, prediction, target = model.flow_matching_loss(
...     lucid.randn((2, 3, 8, 8)))
>>> loss.shape, prediction.shape, target.shape
((), (2, 3, 8, 8), (2, 3, 8, 8))
>>> bool(lucid.allclose(loss, ((prediction - target) ** 2).mean()))
True
notes:
`t` is drawn uniformly per sample, which is the estimator the
objective is written as an expectation over.  Sharing one `t`
across the batch would still be unbiased but noisier.

methods.summary: Generate by integrating the field from noise to data.

parameters.name: n_samples
parameters.description: How many samples to draw.  Ignored when `noise` is given.

parameters.name: steps
parameters.description:
Force a fixed-step solve with this many uniform steps instead
of the adaptive method.  The honest way to report the
few-evaluation sampling the straight paths are supposed to
allow: fix the budget rather than the tolerance.

parameters.name: device
parameters.description:
Where to allocate the prior draw.  Defaults to the device the
model's parameters are on.

parameters.name: noise
parameters.description:
`(N, C, H, W)` starting point, in place of a fresh
standard-normal draw — pass the same tensor to two models to

examples:
>>> import lucid
>>> from lucid.models.generative.flow_matching import (
...     FlowMatchingConfig, FlowMatchingModel,
... )
>>> cfg = FlowMatchingConfig(sample_size=8, base_channels=16,
...                          channel_mult=(1, 2), num_res_blocks=1,
...                          attention_resolutions=(), resnet_groups=8)
>>> model = FlowMatchingModel(cfg).eval()
>>> model.sample(n_samples=2, steps=4).shape
(2, 3, 8, 8)
>>> model.nfe  # the adaptive default falls back to Euler: one call a step

>>> noise = lucid.randn((3, 3, 8, 8))
>>> model.sample(noise=noise, steps=4).shape  # the batch follows noise

methods.name: log_prob
methods.extended:
Integrates the field from `t = 1` back to `t = 0` alongside the
accumulated divergence, then scores the arrival against the
standard normal the path starts from.

parameters.name: x
parameters.description: `(B, C, H, W)` data samples.

examples:
>>> import math
>>> import lucid
>>> from lucid.models.generative.flow_matching import (
...     FlowMatchingConfig, FlowMatchingModel,
... )
>>> cfg = FlowMatchingConfig(sample_size=8, base_channels=16,
...                          channel_mult=(1, 2), num_res_blocks=1,
...                          attention_resolutions=(), resnet_groups=8)
>>> model = FlowMatchingModel(cfg).eval()
>>> x = lucid.randn((2, 3, 8, 8))
>>> log_p = model.log_prob(x)
>>> log_p.shape
(2,)
>>> # A fresh field is exactly zero (its output layer starts at zero),
>>> # so the flow is the identity and x is scored as N(0, I) itself.
>>> const = 0.5 * model.input_dim * math.log(2 * math.pi)
>>> gauss = -0.5 * (x.reshape(2, -1) ** 2).sum(dim=-1) - const
>>> bool(lucid.allclose(log_p, gauss, atol=1e-3))
True
notes:
With `trace_method` resolving to `"hutchinson"` — which it does
at any image size — this is an unbiased *estimate*, and two calls
on the same input will not agree.  That is the same estimator the
paper reports bits/dim with.

methods.name: bits_per_dim
methods.summary: Per-sample negative log-likelihood in bits per dimension.

methods.name: forward
methods.summary: Evaluate the velocity field at `(t, sample)`.

members.summary: Velocity field trained by Conditional Flow Matching.
members.extended:
`forward(sample, t)` evaluates $v_t(x; \theta)$.  The pieces
that make it a generative model are separate and each maps onto one
part of the paper:

* `path_sample` — draw $x_t$ from the conditional path.
* `conditional_target` — the field Theorem 3 says generates it.
* `flow_matching_loss` — the objective, with no solve in it.
* `sample` — integrate $t: 0 \to 1$.
* `log_prob` / `bits_per_dim` — integrate back, tracking
  the divergence.

parameters.name: config
parameters.description: Architecture, path and solver settings.

examples:
>>> import lucid
>>> from lucid.models.generative.flow_matching import (
...     FlowMatchingConfig, FlowMatchingModel,
... )
>>> cfg = FlowMatchingConfig(sample_size=8, base_channels=16,
...                          channel_mult=(1, 2), num_res_blocks=1,
...                          attention_resolutions=(), resnet_groups=8)
>>> model = FlowMatchingModel(cfg).eval()
>>> loss, _, _ = model.flow_matching_loss(lucid.randn((2, 3, 8, 8)))
>>> loss.shape
()
>>> model.sample(n_samples=2, steps=4).shape
(2, 3, 8, 8)
notes:
Reference: Lipman, Chen, Ben-Hamu, Nickel, and Le, *"Flow Matching for
Generative Modeling"*, ICLR, 2023 ([arXiv:2210.02747](https://arxiv.org/abs/2210.02747)).  Theorem 2 gives
the objective's equivalence to the intractable one; Theorem 3 gives
the conditional field; §4.2 gives the optimal-transport path.

**Where to run it.**  Training is a plain U-Net forward and backward
with no solve, so it behaves like any convolutional model and belongs
on `"metal"`.  Sampling and likelihood are solves, and inherit the
same guidance as any continuous flow: the GPU wins once the batch is
real.

summary: Flow Matching family — Lipman et al., 2023 (simulation-free CNF training).
citation: Lipman, Yaron, et al. "Flow Matching for Generative Modeling." International Conference on Learning Representations, 2023.
theory:
A continuous normalizing flow is defined by a vector field: push
samples of a simple distribution along $d\mathbf{x}/dt = v_t(\mathbf{x})$ and read off what arrives.  Training one by maximum
likelihood, as Neural ODE does, means **solving that ODE on every
gradient step** — the cost that kept continuous flows off the scale
diffusion models reached.

Flow Matching removes the solve.  Suppose a probability path
$p_t$ interpolating noise and data were known, together with the
field $u_t$ that generates it; then a regression would suffice,



$$
\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{FM}}(\theta) = \mathbb{E}_{t, p_t(x)}
    \bigl\| v_t(x; \theta) - u_t(x) \bigr\|^2 .
$$

Neither $p_t$ nor $u_t$ is available in closed form.  The
paper's key result — **Theorem 2** — is that they need not be.  Build
the path *per data point*, as a mixture of conditional paths
$p_t(x \mid x_1)$ each generated by a tractable
$u_t(x \mid x_1)$, and regress against the conditional field
instead:



$$
\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{CFM}}(\theta) =
    \mathbb{E}_{t, q(x_1), p_t(x \mid x_1)}
    \bigl\| v_t(x; \theta) - u_t(x \mid x_1) \bigr\|^2 .
$$

The two objectives differ by a constant, so
$\nabla_\theta \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{FM}} = \nabla_\theta \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{CFM}}$.  Training is now a
regression against a target with a closed form: **simulation-free**.

For Gaussian conditional paths $p_t(x \mid x_1) = \mathcal{N}(x \mid \mu_t(x_1), \sigma_t(x_1)^2 I)$, **Theorem 3** names
the unique generating field,



$$
u_t(x \mid x_1) = \frac{\sigma_t'(x_1)}{\sigma_t(x_1)}
    \bigl(x - \mu_t(x_1)\bigr) + \mu_t'(x_1),
$$

so a path is fully specified by two scalar schedules and their
derivatives.  Two instances matter.  The **diffusion** path recovers
the variance-preserving process score-based models use — the
probability path they were already implicitly training, now reachable
by regression.  The **optimal-transport** path takes the schedules
straight,



$$
\mu_t(x_1) = t\,x_1, \qquad
\sigma_t(x_1) = 1 - (1 - \sigma_{\min})\,t,
$$

which makes each conditional flow a constant-speed straight line
between a noise sample and a data point, and collapses the regression
target to something that does not depend on $t$ at all:



$$
\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{CFM}}(\theta) =
    \mathbb{E}_{t, q(x_1), p(x_0)}
    \bigl\| v_t(\psi_t(x_0); \theta)
        - \bigl(x_1 - (1 - \sigma_{\min})\,x_0\bigr) \bigr\|^2,
\qquad
\psi_t(x_0) = \bigl(1 - (1 - \sigma_{\min})t\bigr) x_0 + t\,x_1 .
$$

Diffusion paths bend; these do not, and the particles never overshoot
the target they are heading for.  Straighter trajectories are cheaper
for a solver to follow, which is why sampling needs fewer function
evaluations and why the same solver reaches a better FID.

Time runs from noise to data: $p_0 = \mathcal{N}(0, I)$ and
$p_1 \approx q$.  Sampling integrates $v_t$ from
$t = 0$ to $t = 1$; likelihood integrates the same field
backwards while accumulating $-\operatorname{tr}(\partial v / \partial x)$, exactly as any continuous flow does.
